cards.title: How does a spam folder know?
cards.body:
Your email app quietly moves junk into a spam folder. Nobody wrote a rule for every scam email ever sent. Instead, a [[model]] learned from emails that people had already marked as spam or not spam.

That's [[training data]] at work. In this lesson you'll build some, and find out how easily it goes wrong.

cards.title: Words that vote
cards.body:
This model reads short messages. It remembers which words were in the spam examples and which were in the normal ones.

When a new message arrives, each word in it **votes**. A word gets **one vote for each training message** it appeared in, for that message's label. So if "free" was in three spam messages, it gives spam three votes. A word counts once per message, however many times it's repeated. Words shorter than 3 letters (like "a", "at", "is" and "go") are skipped. Only the **exact same word** counts: to this model, "game" and "games" are different words.

The label with the most votes wins. A tie means "not sure".

cards.prompt:
Be the model. These are its **not spam** training messages:

- See you at training tonight
- Pizza for dinner tonight?
- Can you send me the homework
- Your sister's parcel came today

How many **not spam** votes does **"Free pizza at footy training"** get?
cards.hint: Take the new message one word at a time. For each word, count how many of the four messages contain it. Remember which words are skipped.
cards.nudge: "at" has only 2 letters, so it's skipped. Count only the words of 3 or more letters that appear in the messages.
cards.explanation: "Pizza" is in one message and "training" is in one: **2 votes**. "Free" and "footy" aren't in any of them, and "at" is skipped. The spam messages give "free" 3 votes, so spam will win 3 to 2. Let's see.

cards.prompt: Label each message as **spam** or **not spam**. Then press Check to train the model and see what it makes of two new messages.

examples.text: Your parcel is held, pay the fee here
examples.label: spam

examples.text: Can you send me the homework
examples.label: ok

tests.text: Click to claim a free prize

cards.hint: Spam tries to get you to win, claim, click or pay. Normal messages are about plans and everyday things.
cards.nudge: Look again at the messages about prizes, gift cards and paying a fee: who sends those?
cards.explanation: Your labels were right, and the model called **"Free pizza at footy training"** spam, just as you counted: "free" gave spam 3 votes, and "pizza" and "training" gave not spam only 2.

cards.title: One word, three votes
cards.body:
The model isn't being silly: it did exactly what its training data taught it. In those examples, **"free" only ever appeared in spam**, so to the model, "free" means spam.

Real messages from friends say "free" too: free time, free pizza, free tickets. The training data just didn't show any. A model can't learn from examples it never saw.

cards.prompt: Which **one** new training example would fix the free-pizza mistake, without breaking the spam guess?

options.text: "Free footy training on Saturday", labelled not spam

options.nudge: Count the votes again: a word only counts once per message, however often it's repeated.

options.text: "Win free stuff today, click here", labelled spam
options.nudge: That gives "free" even more spam votes. Which side needs more votes?

options.text: "Pizza night at my place tonight", labelled not spam
options.nudge: Count it: which of its words are in "Free pizza at footy training"? Only one, so it's a tie, not a win.

cards.hint: Count each side's votes for the pizza message, then count again with each new example added.
cards.explanation: "Free footy training on Saturday" adds a not-spam vote for **"free"**, **"footy"** and **"training"**: 5 not-spam votes against 3. "Pizza, pizza, pizza!" only adds **one** vote, because a word counts once per message: that makes a 3-3 tie, "not sure".

cards.prompt: Try it. Choose which examples to train on, so the model gets **both** test messages right.

examples.text: Your parcel is held, pay the fee here
examples.label: spam

examples.text: Can you send me the homework
examples.label: ok

tests.text: Click to claim a free prize

cards.hint: Which side needs more votes from "free"?
cards.nudge: Watch the guess for the pizza message as you tick and untick. A tie shows as "Not sure".
cards.explanation: Adding **"Free footy training on Saturday"** teaches the model that friends say "free" too, so the pizza message gets more not-spam votes. Deleting spam examples can also flip it, but then the model learns less about real spam.

cards.title: Good data, bad data
cards.body:
Training data can go wrong in other ways too:

- **Wrong labels:** a spam message labelled "not spam" teaches the model the wrong lesson.
- **Copies:** a thousand copies of one example add nothing new, and make that one example count far too much.
- **Missing kinds:** examples from only one place, or one kind of person, leave everything else out.

Good training data has **checked labels**, **lots of variety**, and examples like the ones the model will really meet.

cards.prompt: Does each one make training data **better**, or cause a **problem**?

items.label: Messages from lots of different people
Labels checked by a second person
Examples like the ones it will meet
Messages from just one school class
Labels done in a rush, never checked

cards.hint: Ask of each one: does it teach the model something new and true?
cards.nudge: Look for the ones that teach the model something wrong, repeat one example over and over, or leave whole groups out.
cards.explanation: Variety, checked labels and realistic examples make data **better**. Rushed, unchecked labels and spam labelled "not spam" teach wrong lessons; copies add nothing new and tip the votes; one class leaves everyone else out.

cards.prompt: Someone made a labelling mistake in this fruit data. Find it, and choose the examples to train on so the model gets **both** test fruits right. (This model picks the **nearest** example.)
cards.hint: Read each example's name and the label beside it. Does every label match its name?
cards.nudge: Check that every example's label matches its name.
cards.explanation: "Long banana" was labelled **Apple**. It sat closest to the ripe banana, so the model copied its wrong label. Leaving that one example out fixes it: one wrong label can be enough to cause a mistake.

cards.prompt: A spam filter learned only from **English** messages. It lets lots of **Spanish** spam through. Which **one** addition helps most?

options.nudge: That's a lot more data, but does any of it show the model Spanish spam?

options.text: 200 Spanish messages, spam and normal, labelled
200 Spanish spam messages, all labelled spam
options.nudge: Close! But if every Spanish message it sees is spam, what will it think of a friend writing in Spanish?
Copies add nothing new. What's missing from its examples?

cards.hint: Think about what's missing from its examples, and what would happen to normal messages written in Spanish.
cards.explanation: The filter has never seen Spanish, so it needs **Spanish examples**, and **both kinds**: spam only would teach it that Spanish means spam, so friends writing in Spanish would get flagged (like "free" in the pizza message). More English data adds nothing about Spanish.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A model learns only from its **training data**, so it repeats that data's patterns, including its gaps.
- One word, or one example, can tip a model the wrong way.
- Wrong labels, copies and missing kinds of examples all cause mistakes.
- Fix it with **better** data (checked, varied, realistic), not just more of it.

Next: how to tell if a model is any good.
